## Overview {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-note}
## Questions this lesson answers

- How can you search for proteins by free text, gene name, or protein name?
- How do you read the information at the top of a UniProt entry page?
- What kind of information sits behind each download format (FASTA, JSON, XML, GFF)?
- How is the function of a protein such as an opsin described?
- What structured information lives in the *Names and Taxonomy*, *Subcellular location*, *Disease & Variants*, and *PTM/Processing* sections?
- How do you find expression, interaction, structure, family, sequence, and similarity data?
- What do the *Variant viewer* and *Feature viewer* tabs add?
- What does the *Publications* tab list, and how can it be filtered?
- Why does the annotation history of an entry matter?
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Learning objectives

By the end of this session you should be able to:

1. Interpret a UniProtKB entry: function, taxonomy, localisation, structure, interactions, and variants.
2. Use stable unique identifiers to move between databases.
3. Download protein data in an appropriate format for a downstream task.
4. Visualise and compare sequence features along a protein.
:::

| | |
|---|---|
| **Time estimate** | ~1 hour |
| **Level** | Introductory |
| **Prerequisites** | Basic familiarity with genes, proteins, and FASTA files |
| **Software needed** | A web browser only |

: Practical details {.striped .hover tbl-colwidths="[25,75]"}

::: {.callout-caution appearance="simple"}
Numbers reported in the solutions below (counts of search hits, publications,
variants, and so on) were correct when the lesson was written. UniProt is
updated roughly every eight weeks, so your numbers may differ. That is a
feature, not a bug.

Ask yourself: Why does a knowledge base change?
:::

## Why bother with UniProt? {#sec-intro}

A typical analysis ends with a shortlist of interesting proteins. Then what?
You need to find out what those proteins do, where they act, what is already
known about their variants, and which other databases hold complementary
information.

This lesson uses **human opsins** as a worked example. Opsins sit in the cells
of the retina, where they capture light and start the signalling cascade that
produces vision. When they are disrupted, the result can be colour blindness or
other visual impairment.

Almost all of the work happens on the [UniProt](https://www.uniprot.org)
website rather than in any analysis platform, so nothing needs installing.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Sources and further reading

The original Galaxy Training Network lesson drew on the UniProt help page
[Explore UniProtKB entry](https://www.uniprot.org/help/explore_uniprotkb_entry),
and chose the topic following Gale Rhodes'
[Bioinformatics Tutorial](https://spdbv.unil.ch/TheMolecularLevel/Matics/index.html).
The latter can no longer be followed step by step (the resources have changed
too much) but is still a good source of background on opsins and on building
structural models from evolutionary information.
:::

## Finding the right entry {#sec-search}

The starting point for protein annotation is [UniProtKB](https://www.uniprot.org/).
You can query it with free text, a gene name, or a protein name. Let us begin
with something deliberately vague.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔬 Hands on: a broad search

1. Open <https://www.uniprot.org/>.
2. Type `Human opsin` into the search bar.
3. Run the search.
:::

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

How many results come back?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
Around 524 at the time of writing. Far too many to inspect by hand, even
though (spoiler) the entry we want is near the top.
:::
::::

Free text is too blunt an instrument. A better strategy is to search on a
**unique identifier**. The gene we are after is `OPN1LW`.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔬 Hands on: search by gene name

1. Type `OPN1LW` into the search bar.
2. Run the search.
:::

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

1. How many results now?
2. What is still missing from the query?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
1. Over 240 results.
2. The organism. The same gene name is used across many species, so add
   `Human` to restrict the search.
:::
::::

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔬 Hands on: search by gene name plus organism

1. Type `Human OPN1LW` into the search bar.
2. Run the search.
:::

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

1. How many results now?
2. Is there a hit whose gene name is exactly OPN1LW?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
1. Eight results.
2. Yes. The first hit carries the label `Gene: OPN1LW (RCP)`.
:::
::::

That first hit, **P04000 (OPSR_HUMAN)**, is our target. Two things are worth
noticing before opening it:

- The protein name (`OPSR_HUMAN`) and the gene name (`OPN1LW`) are different,
  and so are their identifiers. Gene and protein are distinct entities with
  distinct names.
- The entry carries a gold star, meaning it has been manually annotated and
  curated by a human (Swiss-Prot) rather than generated automatically (via TrEMBL).

## Reading the entry page {#sec-entry}

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔬 Hands on: open the entry

Click on `P04000 · OPSR_HUMAN`, or go directly to
<https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P04000/entry>.
:::

![The header of a UniProt entry page. Image from the Galaxy Training Network lesson, CC BY 4.0.](https://training.galaxyproject.org/training-material/topics/data-science/tutorials/online-resources-protein/images/UniProt.png){#fig-uniprot fig-alt="Screenshot of the UniProt entry page header for P04000."}

<!-- Tip for reuse: download this image and store it locally, e.g. in an
     images/ folder next to this .qmd, rather than hotlinking. Keep the
     CC BY 4.0 credit in the caption. -->

The page is long, so the left-hand navigation bar does a lot of work. It stays
fixed as you scroll, and just reading it tells you what the database holds
about this entry:

::: {.grid}
::: {.g-col-6}
- known functions
- taxonomy
- subcellular location
- variants and associated diseases
- post-translational modifications (PTMs)
:::
::: {.g-col-6}
- expression
- interactions
- structure
- domains and their classification
- sequences and similar proteins
:::
:::

At the very top of the page you get the accession and entry name, the protein
and gene names, the organism, whether the entry has been reviewed by a curator,
an annotation score, and the evidence level for the protein's existence.

Below the header sit six tabs: *Entry*, *Variant viewer*, *Feature viewer*,
*Publications*, *External links*, and *History*. Stay on *Entry* for now.

### Downloading the entry {#sec-download}

Just under the tabs there is a toolbar. From here you can BLAST the sequence,
align it against its isoforms, add the entry to a basket for later, or download
it.

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

1. Which formats does the *Download* menu offer?
2. What sort of information does each one carry?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
1. Text, FASTA (canonical), FASTA (canonical and isoform), JSON, XML, RDF/XML,
   and GFF.
2. The FASTA options give you the sequence, optionally as a multi-FASTA that
   includes isoforms. The rest are general-purpose structured formats, not
   biology-specific: they carry the same annotation you are reading on the page,
   but in a form that a script can parse. JSON is usually the most convenient
   for programmatic work.
:::
::::

### Function {#sec-function}

The *Function* section opens with a short free-text summary: visual pigments
are the light-absorbing molecules behind vision, and consist of an apoprotein
(opsin) covalently bound to cis-retinal.

Two sentences to stand in for decades of literature. That compression is
possible because someone has already done the curation work, and because the
protein has been classified in the **Gene Ontology** (GO), which describes
molecular function, biological process, and cellular component.

GO is a good example of a resource that flattens a very complex body of
knowledge into a graph. Detail is lost, but in exchange the information becomes
countable, comparable, and machine-readable, which is exactly what makes summary
pages like this one possible.

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

Which GO terms is this protein annotated with, for:

1. molecular function?
2. cellular component?
3. biological process?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
1. Photoreceptor protein, G-protein coupled receptor.
2. Photoreceptor disc membrane.
3. Sensory transduction, vision.
:::
::::

### Names and taxonomy {#sec-names}

The next section holds more structured information, including the taxonomic
placement of the protein. It also lists other identifiers that point at the same
biological entity, or at linked entities (for example associated diseases under
`MIM`).

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

1. What is the taxonomic identifier?
2. What is the proteome identifier?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
1. 9606, that is *Homo sapiens*.
2. UP000005640, and this protein is a component of chromosome X.
:::
::::

### Subcellular location {#sec-location}

We already know where the protein is in the body (the retina). Where is it in
the cell?

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

1. Where does UniProt place this protein within the cell?
2. Is that consistent with the GO annotation you saw earlier?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
1. It is described as a multi-pass membrane protein: it is embedded in the
   membrane and crosses it several times.
2. Yes. GO is more specific, naming the photoreceptor disc membrane.
:::
::::

This section also has a *Features* area showing which stretches of the sequence
sit inside the membrane (transmembrane) and which do not (topological domain).

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

How many transmembrane and topological domains are listed?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
Eight transmembrane regions and seven topological domains.
:::
::::

### Disease and variants {#sec-disease}

This gene and protein are linked to several diseases. The section describes
those associations and lists the specific variants implicated in each.

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

What kinds of study establish that a genetic variant is associated with a
disease?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
Three common designs:

- **Genome-wide association studies (GWAS).** Scan whole genomes across large
  cohorts to find common variants that track with a trait or disease.
- **Case-control studies.** Compare the frequency of specific variants between
  affected and unaffected individuals.
- **Family studies.** Follow inheritance patterns within families in which
  several members are affected, which can pinpoint candidate genes.

All of these lean heavily on genomic file formats such as SAM, BAM, and VCF.
:::
::::

A *Features* area maps the natural variants along the sequence, and points you
to the fuller view in the *Variant viewer* tab. Resist the temptation for now.

### PTM and processing {#sec-ptm}

A post-translational modification is a covalent event after translation: either
a proteolytic cleavage, or the addition of a chemical group to an amino acid.

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

Which post-translational modifications are annotated here?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
Chain, glycosylation, disulfide bond, and modified residue.
:::
::::

### Expression {#sec-expression}

For human proteins there is often tissue-level expression information, drawn
from resources such as the [Expression Atlas](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/gxa/home).

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

In which tissue is this protein found?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
The three colour pigments are found in the cone photoreceptor cells.
:::
::::

### Interaction {#sec-interaction}

Proteins do their work by interacting with their surroundings, and above all
with other proteins. This section lists known interactors in a table you can
filter by subcellular location, disease, and interaction type. Much of the
underlying data comes from databases such as STRING, which is linked directly.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔬 Hands on: follow the link out to STRING

Open the [STRING network for this protein](https://string-db.org/network/9606.ENSP00000358967)
in a new tab.
:::

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

1. How many download formats does STRING offer?
2. What does each one carry?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
STRING exports interaction data in several shapes:

- **TSV**, a tabular layout that drops straight into analysis tools.
- **PSI-MI XML**, a community standard for interaction data, which makes the
  results interoperable with other interaction databases.
- **PNG and SVG** images of the network, for slides and figures.
- **Flat files** with detailed interaction evidence, and multiple alignment
  files for comparing sequences across the network.
:::
::::

### Structure {#sec-structure}

The *Structure* section is the way into the three-dimensional world. It reports
experimentally determined structures where they exist, and gives you an
interactive viewer embedded in the page, so you can rotate the molecule and
explore domains, binding sites, and other functional regions without leaving
UniProt.

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

1. Which variant is associated with colour blindness?
2. Can you locate that amino acid in the structure?
3. Why might that substitution be disruptive?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
1. From the *Disease & Variants* section: a glycine to glutamic acid change at
   position 338.
2. Yes. Rotate the model and hover over residues to find position 338. It takes
   patience given how many helices there are. Residue 338 is not in a helix, but
   in what looks like a loop, just before a region of low prediction confidence.
3. A reasonable hypothesis: since it is not in a helix, and helices in
   transmembrane proteins are usually the membrane-spanning parts, this residue
   is in one of the larger domains protruding from the membrane. So the mutation
   probably disturbs a functional domain rather than the membrane-embedded core.
   Use the *Feature viewer* to check whether that domain faces the inside or the
   outside of the cell.
:::
::::

Where does the model actually come from?

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔬 Hands on: download the structure

1. Click the download icon underneath the structure viewer.
2. Open the downloaded file in a text editor and look at the first few lines.
:::

You get a **PDB** file, describing the arrangement of atoms and residues. But
notice that the list of 3D structure databases does not link to the Protein Data
Bank first. It links to **AlphaFoldDB**.

That matters. This is a *predicted* structure, not an experimentally determined
one. AlphaFold infers the spatial arrangement of atoms using deep learning and
evolutionary information. It is also why the model is coloured by confidence:
blue regions are predicted reliably, orange regions are either uncertain or
genuinely disordered (flexible and mobile). The file format is the same as for
an experimental structure, because the information it encodes is still
structural, but the epistemic status is very different.

::: {.callout-important collapse="true"}
## Teaching note

This is a good moment to stop and discuss provenance with students. Two files
can look identical in format while differing completely in how much you should
trust them. Ask: how would you record that distinction in your own project
metadata?
:::

### Family and domains {#sec-family}

This section places the protein in its evolutionary context: the families,
superfamilies, and domains it belongs to, plus conserved regions, motifs, and
other notable sequence features.

The *Features* area confirms that at least one of the two protruding domains
(the N-terminal one) is disordered, and reiterates that we are dealing with a
transmembrane protein. The links out to phylogenetic and domain databases are
the route into questions of common ancestry and functional specialisation.

### Sequence {#sec-sequence}

Everything above is ultimately encoded in the sequence. Here you can download
the FASTA file, trace the data back to the sequencing experiments that produced
it, and see any isoforms that have been detected.

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

How many potential isoforms map to this entry?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
One: H0Y622.
:::
::::

### Similar proteins {#sec-similar}

The final section of the *Entry* tab lists similar proteins, produced by
clustering at 100%, 90%, and 50% identity thresholds.

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

How many similar proteins are there at each threshold?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
| Identity threshold | Similar proteins |
|---|---|
| 100% | 0 |
| 90% | 83 |
| 50% | 397 |

: Cluster membership {.striped}
:::
::::

A pattern should be emerging: much of what we do with protein data is mapping
different layers of information onto the same sequence and asking how they
relate. The next two tabs do exactly that, visually.

## Variant viewer {#sec-variant-viewer}

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔬 Hands on

Click the *Variant viewer* tab.
:::

This view maps every known alternative version of the sequence. Some have a
known effect (pathogenic or benign); many do not.

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

How many variants are flagged as likely pathogenic?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
Zoom out and count the red points: five.
:::
::::

The sheer number of variants is a useful corrective. A "protein sequence" (like
a gene sequence, or a structure) is much less of a fixed object than the
singular canonical entry suggests.

## Feature viewer {#sec-feature-viewer}

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔬 Hands on

Click the *Feature viewer* tab.
:::

The *Feature viewer* merges all the *Features* areas scattered through the
*Entry* page into one track-based display: domains and sites, molecule
processing, PTMs, topology, proteomics, and variants. Clicking a feature
highlights the corresponding region in the structure.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔬 Hands on: locate the variant in context

1. Expand the *Variants* track.
2. Zoom out.
3. Click the red point at position 338.
:::

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

What is the topology at that position?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
It falls in a topological cytoplasmic domain, so on the inside of the cell.
This also answers the open question from @sec-structure.
:::
::::

## Publications {#sec-publications}

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔬 Hands on

Click the *Publications* tab.
:::

This tab lists papers relevant to the protein, combining a manually curated list
(from UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot) with automatically imported references. You can
filter by source, by the category of data a paper contributes (function,
interaction, sequence, and so on), and by study size (small scale versus large
scale).

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

1. How many publications are linked to this protein?
2. How many of them contribute information about its function?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
1. 57.
2. 23.
:::
::::

## External links {#sec-external}

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔬 Hands on

Click the *External links* tab.
:::

This tab gathers every cross-reference scattered across the entry into one
place. The link text usually shows the identifier that represents the same
entity in the other database, which is what makes automated cross-referencing
possible at all.

For a sense of how tangled that web is, look at the bioDBnet network diagram
([source](https://biodbnet-abcc.ncifcrf.gov/dbInfo/netGraph.php)). Databases are
the major nodes, identifiers the minor ones, and the region around the UniProt
entry name, Gene ID, and Ensembl Gene ID is extremely dense. The diagram is
already partly out of date, which rather makes the point.

## History {#sec-history}

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔬 Hands on

Click the *History* tab.
:::

The *History* tab exposes every previous version of the entry's annotation, in
this case going back to 1988, and lets you download them. It is a record of how
knowledge about this protein has accumulated and been revised.

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

Was this entry ever *not* manually annotated?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
Scroll back through the table and check the `Database` column. It never sits in
TrEMBL, only in Swiss-Prot, so the entry has been manually curated from the
start.
:::
::::

## Key points {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Take home messages

- UniProtKB entries collect function, taxonomy, localisation, interactions, and
  much more in one curated place.
- Search on unique identifiers, not free text, whenever you can.
- The *Variant viewer* and *Feature viewer* let you see variants, domains,
  modifications, and topology mapped onto the sequence.
- External links and shared identifiers are what let you cross-reference between
  resources.
- The *History* tab shows that annotation is a moving target, not a fixed fact.
:::

## Exercises to extend the session {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Suggested follow-up (edit or remove these for your own course)

1. Repeat the whole walk-through for `OPN1MW` (medium-wave opsin) or `RHO`
   (rhodopsin) and note where the entries differ in evidence level and
   annotation score.
2. Download the JSON for P04000 and write a short script that extracts every
   annotated transmembrane region as a table.
3. Compare the AlphaFold model with an experimentally determined GPCR structure
   of your choice. Where do the confidence estimates and the experimental data
   agree?
4. Pick one paper from the *Publications* tab and trace which annotations in the
   entry it supports.
:::
